questions.text:
Derive the mathematical relationship between the elastic constants: Young's Modulus ($E$), Shear Modulus ($G$), Bulk Modulus ($K$), and Poisson's ratio ($
u$): $E = 2G(1+
u) = 3K(1-2
u) =  rac{9KG}{3K+G}$.

For a two-dimensional state of plane stress subjected to normal stresses $\sigma_x, \sigma_y$ and shear stress $\tau_{xy}$, determine: (a) Principal stresses $\sigma_1, \sigma_2$ and orientation of principal planes, (b) Maximum in-plane shearing stress $\tau_{\max}$, and (c) Verify results using Mohr's Circle of stress.

For a given unsymmetrical structural section (angle section, Z-section, channel section), determine centroid $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$, moments of inertia $I_x, I_y$, product of inertia $I_{xy}$, and calculate principal moments of inertia ($I_u, I_v$) and orientation of principal axes.

Prove that circumferential (hoop) stress in a thin cylinder subjected to internal fluid pressure $p$ is twice the longitudinal stress ($\sigma_h = \frac{pd}{2t}, \sigma_L = \frac{pd}{4t}$). Derive formulas for volumetric strain and change in internal volume.

Derive the torsion formula $\frac{T}{J} = \frac{\tau}{R} = \frac{G\theta}{L}$. Prove that a hollow circular shaft has greater torque transmission capacity and stiffness than a solid shaft of identical weight and material cross-sectional area.

A hollow steel shaft having outer diameter $D$ and inner diameter $d$ transmits specified power at given RPM. If maximum shear stress is limited to $\tau_{\text{allow}}$ and twist angle to $\theta_{\text{allow}}$, determine suitable shaft dimensions.

State the assumptions and derive Euler's formula for the critical buckling load of an ideal column of length $L$ and flexural rigidity $EI$ with: (a) Both ends hinged ($P_{\text{cr}} = \frac{\pi^2 EI}{L^2}$), and (b) One end fixed and other end free ($P_{\text{cr}} = \frac{\pi^2 EI}{4L^2}$).
Determine the slope and deflection at the free end of a cantilever beam or at the center of a simply supported beam subjected to point loads and UDL using Macaulay's method or Moment-Area theorems.
A rigid bar $ABC$ is hinged at one end and supported by vertical steel and copper/aluminum rods. Determine the forces developed in each rod and vertical displacement under an applied vertical load.
Derive the horizontal shear stress formula in a beam cross-section: $\tau = \frac{V Q}{I b}$. Plot the shear stress distribution across the depth of an I-beam, T-beam, and rectangular beam.

For a given planar frame carrying concentrated loads and UDL, compute support reactions and draw Axial Force Diagram (AFD), Shear Force Diagram (SFD), and Bending Moment Diagram (BMD) indicating salient points and points of contraflexure.
Derive the expression for total elongation of a uniformly tapering circular bar of length $L$ tapering from diameter $d_1$ to $d_2$ under axial tensile load $P$: $\delta = \frac{4PL}{\pi E d_1 d_2}$.

A compound bar consisting of a steel tube and an internal copper rod is rigidly connected at both ends. Determine the thermal stresses developed in steel and copper when the temperature rises by $\Delta T$.
Derive the flexure formula for pure bending of beams: $\frac{M}{I} = \frac{\sigma}{y} = \frac{E}{R}$. Define section modulus ($Z$) and moment of resistance.
State and prove the Parallel Axis Theorem for product of inertia ($I_{xy} = I_{\bar{x}\bar{y}} + A \bar{x}\bar{y}$).

Explain the limitations of Euler's formula for short and intermediate columns. Derive the Rankine-Gordon empirical formula $\frac{1}{P_R} = \frac{1}{P_c} + \frac{1}{P_e}$ and define slenderness ratio.

Derive the Bending Formula (Flexure formula) for beams under pure bending: $\frac{M}{I} = \frac{\sigma}{y} = \frac{E}{R}$. State assumptions in Euler-Bernoulli beam theory and define Section Modulus ($Z$).
questions.solutionOutline: Assumptions: plane sections remain plane after bending, beam material is homogeneous, isotropic, obeys Hooke law, radius of curvature R >> beam depth. Longitudinal strain epsilon = y / R. Stress sigma = E y / R. Equating internal moment of resistance M = integral sigma y dA = (E / R) integral y^2 dA = (E / R) I => M / I = sigma / y = E / R. Section modulus Z = I / y_max; maximum bending stress sigma_max = M / Z.

questions.text: Derive the Shear Stress formula for beams: $\tau = \frac{V Q}{I b}$. Plot the shear stress distribution across rectangular, circular, I-section, and T-section beam profiles.
questions.solutionOutline: Consider longitudinal equilibrium of differential slice dx above level y: dF = (dM / I) integral y dA. Horizontal shear force dF must balance shear stress tau * b * dx => tau = (dM/dx) Q / (I b) = V Q / (I b), where Q = first moment of area above level y. For rectangular section (b x d): parabolic distribution with tau_max = 1.5 (V / A) at neutral axis. For circular section: tau_max = (4/3) (V / A). For I-section: flange carries tiny shear; web carries >90% of total shear with step jump at flange-web junction.

questions.text: Derive the Torsion Equation for circular solid and hollow shafts: $\frac{T}{J} = \frac{\tau}{r} = \frac{G \theta}{L}$. Calculate the power transmitted $P = \frac{2\pi N T}{60}$ and polar section modulus ($Z_p$) for a solid shaft.
questions.solutionOutline: Assumptions: circular cross-sections remain circular and plane, shear strain proportional to radius gamma = r theta / L. Shear stress tau = G gamma = G r theta / L. Resisting torque T = integral tau r dA = (G theta / L) integral r^2 dA = (G theta / L) J => T / J = tau / r = G theta / L. Polar moment J = pi d^4 / 32. Polar section modulus Z_p = J / R = pi d^3 / 16. Power P = omega T = 2 pi N T / 60 watts.

questions.text: Derive the Differential Equation of Beam Deflection $E I \frac{d^2 y}{dx^2} = M(x)$. Apply Macaulay's Method to find slope and deflection at the center of a simply supported beam with asymmetric point loads.
questions.solutionOutline: From curvature relation 1/R = d^2 y / dx^2 and M = E I / R: EI d^2y/dx^2 = M(x). Macaulay method writes unified bending moment expression across entire span using bracket notation [x - a]^n, valid only when x > a. First integration gives slope EI dy/dx = C1 + ... Second integration gives deflection EI y = C1 x + C2 + ... Boundary conditions y(0) = 0 and y(L) = 0 solve for constants C1 and C2 directly.

questions.text: Apply Moment-Area Theorems (Mohr's Theorems) and Conjugate Beam Method to calculate the maximum deflection and slope for a cantilever beam carrying an end point load and uniformly distributed load.
questions.solutionOutline: Mohr Theorem 1: angle change between two points theta_B - theta_A equals area of M/(EI) diagram between them. Mohr Theorem 2: tangential deviation t_{B/A} equals first moment of M/(EI) diagram area about B. Conjugate beam: real beam fixed support becomes free, free end becomes fixed. Bending moment in conjugate beam equals deflection in real beam; shear force in conjugate beam equals slope in real beam. For cantilever with end load P: theta_max = P L^2 / (2 EI); delta_max = P L^3 / (3 EI).

questions.text: Derive Euler's Critical Buckling Load for an ideal column with both ends hinged: $P_{cr} = \frac{\pi^2 E I}{L^2}$. State effective lengths ($L_e$) for various end conditions and explain the slenderness ratio limitation ($\lambda = L_e / r_{min}$).
questions.solutionOutline: Governing ODE: EI d^2y/dx^2 + P y = 0 => y(x) = A cos(k x) + B sin(k x), where k = sqrt(P / EI). Boundary conditions y(0) = 0 => A = 0; y(L) = 0 => B sin(k L) = 0 => k L = n pi => P_cr = pi^2 EI / L^2. Effective lengths: both hinged Le = L; one fixed one free Le = 2L; both fixed Le = 0.5L; one fixed one hinged Le = L / sqrt(2) approx 0.707L. Critical stress sigma_cr = pi^2 E / lambda^2; valid only when sigma_cr <= proportional limit (long slender columns, lambda > 80-100 for steel).

questions.text: Explain the Rankine-Gordon Formula for intermediate columns: $\frac{1}{P_R} = \frac{1}{P_c} + \frac{1}{P_E}$. Show that $P_R = \frac{\sigma_c A}{1 + a (L_e / r)^2}$ and compare with Euler's buckling curve.
questions.solutionOutline: Combines crushing failure (short columns P_c = sigma_c A) and buckling failure (long columns P_E = pi^2 EI / Le^2). 1/P_R = 1/P_c + 1/P_E => P_R = (P_c * P_E) / (P_c + P_E) = P_c / [1 + P_c / P_E]. Substituting P_E gives Rankine formula P_R = (sigma_c A) / [1 + a (Le / r)^2], where a = sigma_c / (pi^2 E) is Rankine constant. Applicable to both short, intermediate, and long columns.

questions.text: Derive formulas for Circumferential (Hoop) Stress $\sigma_h = \frac{p d}{2t}$ and Longitudinal Stress $\sigma_l = \frac{p d}{4t}$ in a thin cylindrical pressure vessel under internal fluid pressure $p$. Calculate maximum shear stress and volumetric strain.
questions.solutionOutline: Thin cylinder has t/d < 1/20. Hoop stress: balance bursting force p * d * L against resisting force 2 * sigma_h * t * L => sigma_h = p d / (2t). Longitudinal stress: balance end pressure p * pi d^2 / 4 against wall tension sigma_l * pi d t => sigma_l = p d / (4t) = sigma_h / 2. Maximum in-plane shear stress tau_max = (sigma_h - sigma_l)/2 = p d / (8t); absolute max shear = sigma_h / 2 = p d / (4t). Volumetric strain Delta V / V = 2 epsilon_h + epsilon_l = (p d / 4t E)(5 - 4 nu).

questions.text: Derive expressions for Principal Stresses ($\sigma_1, \sigma_2$), maximum shear stress $\tau_{max} = \frac{\sigma_1 - \sigma_2}{2}$, and principal plane angle ($\theta_p$) for a 2D stress element ($\sigma_x, \sigma_y, \tau_{xy}$). Draw and explain Mohr's Circle of Stresses.
questions.solutionOutline: Normal stress on inclined plane at angle theta: sigma_theta = (sigma_x + sigma_y)/2 + (sigma_x - sigma_y)/2 cos(2 theta) + tau_xy sin(2 theta). Shear stress tau_theta = -(sigma_x - sigma_y)/2 sin(2 theta) + tau_xy cos(2 theta). Setting d sigma / d theta = 0 gives tan(2 theta_p) = 2 tau_xy / (sigma_x - sigma_y). Principal stresses sigma_{1,2} = (sigma_x + sigma_y)/2 +/- sqrt[((sigma_x - sigma_y)/2)^2 + tau_xy^2]. Mohr circle: center at ((sigma_x + sigma_y)/2, 0), radius R = tau_max.

questions.text: Explain Theories of Failure for isotropic ductile and brittle materials: Maximum Principal Stress Theory (Rankine), Maximum Shear Stress Theory (Tresca), and Maximum Distortion Energy Theory (von Mises).
questions.solutionOutline: Predicts yielding/fracture under multi-axial stress. Rankine: failure occurs when max principal stress sigma_1 >= sigma_y (accurate for brittle materials: cast iron, concrete). Tresca: yielding occurs when max shear stress tau_max = (sigma_1 - sigma_3)/2 >= sigma_y / 2 (conservative for ductile materials). Von Mises: yielding occurs when distortion energy per unit volume exceeds yield value in simple tension: (sigma1 - sigma2)^2 + (sigma2 - sigma3)^2 + (sigma3 - sigma1)^2 >= 2 sigma_y^2 (most accurate for ductile metals).

questions.text:
Derive the relationships between Elastic Constants: Young's Modulus of Elasticity ($E$), Shear Modulus ($G$), Bulk Modulus ($K$), and Poisson's Ratio ($
u$): $E = 2G(1 + 
u) = 3K(1 - 2
u)$.
questions.solutionOutline: Consider unit cube subjected to hydrostatic stress sigma: volumetric strain epsilon_v = 3 epsilon_x = 3 [sigma/E - 2 nu sigma/E] = 3 sigma (1 - 2 nu) / E. By definition bulk modulus K = sigma / epsilon_v = E / [3 (1 - 2 nu)] => E = 3K(1 - 2 nu). For pure shear tau, state of stress is equivalent to tensile and compressive stresses tau at 45 deg. Principal strain epsilon_1 = tau/E + nu tau/E = (tau / 2G) => E = 2G(1 + nu). Combining yields G = 3K(1 - 2 nu) / [2 (1 + nu)].

questions.text: Calculate Thermal Stresses and strains developed in a composite bar made of copper and steel components rigidly connected together at both ends when subjected to a uniform temperature change $\Delta T$.
questions.solutionOutline: Coefficient of thermal expansion of copper alpha_c > alpha_s (steel). Free thermal expansion Delta L_c = L alpha_c Delta T > Delta L_s = L alpha_s Delta T. Rigid connection forces equal final elongation Delta L: steel is pulled into tension (stress sigma_s), copper is pushed into compression (stress sigma_c). Equilibrium: P_s = P_c => sigma_s A_s = sigma_c A_c. Compatibility: Delta L_c - sigma_c L / E_c = Delta L_s + sigma_s L / E_s. Solve simultaneous equations for sigma_s and sigma_c.

questions.text: State the Parallel Axis Theorem and Perpendicular Axis Theorem. Calculate the centroid and second moments of area ($I_{xx}, I_{yy}$) of an asymmetrical T-section or channel section.
questions.solutionOutline: Parallel axis theorem: I_x = I_G + A d^2, where I_G is moment of inertia about centroidal axis, d is distance between parallel axes. Perpendicular axis theorem (for planar laminas): I_z = I_x + I_y. For T-section (flange b x tf, web tw x hw): find centroid y_bar = (A1 y1 + A2 y2) / (A1 + A2). Compute I_xx = (b tf^3 / 12 + A1 d1^2) + (tw hw^3 / 12 + A2 d2^2). I_yy = (tf b^3 / 12) + (hw tw^3 / 12).

questions.text: Draw the Shear Force Diagram (SFD) and Bending Moment Diagram (BMD) for a simply supported beam with an overhang carrying a uniformly distributed load and point loads. Identify points of zero shear, maximum positive/negative bending moments, and points of contraflexure.
questions.solutionOutline: 1) Calculate support reactions using static equilibrium equations sum F_y = 0 and sum M = 0. 2) Formulate SF equations across each span segment; SF is constant under point load, slopes linearly under UDL. 3) Find section where SF = 0 (critical section of maximum bending moment). 4) Formulate BM equations (linear under point loads, parabolic under UDL). 5) Find point of contraflexure where M(x) = 0, indicating curvature reversal from sagging to hogging.
